sources.quote: The name "baryon", introduced by Abraham Pais, comes from the Greek word for "heavy" (βαρύς, barýs), because, at the time of their naming, most known elementary particles had lower masses than the baryons.
Baryons (three quarks) have B = +1, mesons (one quark, one antiquark) have B = 0, and antibaryons (three antiquarks) have B = −1.
Protons are spin-1/2 fermions and are composed of three valence quarks, making them baryons (a sub-type of hadrons).

notes: Dev-split ABox expansion paired with physics-replace-d001 ("The muon is a baryon."): the same relation (in_particle_family) and new object, with a made-up subject (fictional: subject) in an empty slot; new baryons are reported every year, so nothing real is contradicted. "Dravellon" has 0 hits in Dolma and Wikipedia, and sounds like no real family. Direct, paraphrase and cross-lingual are the revision's questions with the new subject, naming the two options (lepton or baryon). The three derived questions mirror the revision's: the chain to hadron, the meaning of the Greek root of the family name (composition), and the total baryon number of a sample (inheritance, application, arithmetic). All bridges, checks and evidence are the revision's. Quark-count questions were avoided because pentaquarks are baryons too. The near unrelated question asks the tau's family, whose reference (lepton) differs from the new answer.
